data.title: Middle East Eye: NAZA: Israeli embassies in UK and US promote rival documentary to challenge Gaza genocide allegations
data.author: Katherine Hearst
data.summary:
NAZA: Israeli embassies in UK and US promote rival documentary to challenge Gaza genocide allegations
Israeli embassies in the United States and the United Kingdom are promoting a copycat NAZA, nearly a month after the release of the original that focuses on testimony of Israelis killing Palestinians in Gaza.
In posts on X, the embassies said that "Naza: The Real Story" is "setting the record straight" and claims to offer a firsthand account from senior Israeli military commanders and intelligence officers directly involved in Israel's genocidal war on Gaza.
It said the film uses combat footage, declassified materials, captured intelligence and firsthand testimony to give context on "how the war was fought and the challenges Israeli forces faced".
The film's website names the provider as Three Musketeers Production, "a company in formation", and says a registered address and registration number will be published once the company is registered. It says the directors are deliberately not named "for their safety".
Claimed to have been filmed on the rooftops of Tel Aviv, the 49-minute documentary is available in 17 languages on its official website.
Read more: NAZA: Israeli embassies in UK and US promote rival documentary to challenge Gaza genocide allegations

Al Jazeera reports, citing the Palestine Red Crescent Society, that 41-year-old Raafat Khairi Ahmed Abu Khalil was killed by Israeli soldiers at the Anab checkpoint east of Tulkarm in the occupied West Bank.
Citing sources at Nasser Medical Complex, the report said that another Palestinian had been killed in Israeli shelling northwest of southern Gaza's Khan Younis.
The last month has seen a surge in Israeli attacks across Gaza despite a so-called ceasefire which came into effect in October last year.

data.author: MEE and agencies

The 46,000-seat venue was planned 350 metres above ground inside The Line, one of Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman's flagship projects
A design plan for The Line, a proposed 500-metre-tall development in Saudi Arabia’s Neom project, 26 July 2022 (Neom/AFP)
Off
Saudi Arabia has quietly shelved plans for a $2.5bn stadium planned as a venue for the 2034 Fifa World Cup, as delays to the country's flagship Neom development cast doubt over some of the kingdom's most ambitious projects.
Reuters reported that the $2.5bn stadium construction was suspended, according to MEED Projects, a construction intelligence platform, which classified the project as “on hold” with no end date.
The stadium was set to be one of the most futuristic sports venues in Saudi Arabia’s World Cup plans, located 350 metres above ground level within the 160 km-long Neom development.
In 2024, Saudi Arabia unveiled its 2034 World Cup venue plans, with the Neom stadium among 15 proposed venues across five cities.
MEED said at the time that the stadium would seat 46,000 spectators and would be built within The Line.
Fifa chose Saudi Arabia to host the 2034 World Cup in December 2024. The tournament, which will feature 48 teams, will be the first of its kind to be played out in one country.
The latest developments cast a shadow over The Line, the new masterplan at the heart of Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s Vision 2030 economic transformation plan, which has seen the kingdom embark on an ambitious agenda of futuristic developments.
Yasir Al-Rumayyan, governor of the Public Investment Fund (PIF), which owns Neom, said in April that The Line was no longer a priority and not of utmost importance before 2030, although he stopped short of confirming that any projects had been cancelled.

data.title: Middle East Eye: As olive harvest nears, Palestinian farmers urgently need international protection
data.author: Fareed Taamallah
data.summary:
As olive harvest nears, Palestinian farmers urgently need international protection
Submitted by
Fareed Taamallah
on
Tue, 09/29/2026 - 14:23
Settlers armed and shielded by Israel are driving West Bank olive farmers off ancestral land. Sanctions on a handful of them will not stop the next attack
Israeli military machinery uproots olive trees in the village of Beit Rima, near Ramallah, in the occupied West Bank, on 24 September 2026 (Reuters/Ali Sawafta)
Off
Every October, the ancient olive groves in my hometown and across the occupied West Bank become dynamic hubs of life and labour. For generations of Palestinians, the olive harvest has been the pulse of our economic survival and a living link to our ancestors. The olive tree, resilient and deep-rooted, is a symbol of who we are and of our connection to this land.
As this year's harvest approaches, our villages are gripped by a dread I have not seen before. In recent weeks, the situation across the West Bank has deteriorated sharply. Military raids, arbitrary road closures and daily incursions by armed settler militias have turned our countryside into a militarised zone.
This season is shaping up to be worse than any we have faced. With Israeli elections set for 27 October, political factions are openly competing over who can strike the most aggressive posture towards Palestinians.
Settlers are better armed than ever, equipped with assault rifles and military gear, and backed by state institutions. Before a single olive has been picked, settler violence has already reached record levels, with the UN recording an average of more than six attacks a day in August.
This terror hits close to home. In my village of Qira, in the Salfit governorate, my family and neighbours await the harvest with deep anxiety. Our ancestral groves, like those in surrounding villages, are targeted by the illegal settlements and outposts around them.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Green Party recognises Zionism as a form of racism and backs single Palestinian state
data.author: Katherine Hearst
data.summary:
Green Party recognises Zionism as a form of racism and backs single Palestinian state
The Green Party of England and Wales has voted to declare Zionism a form of racism in an unprecedented move at its party conference in Brighton, Middle East Eye has learnt.
The vote by party members on Sunday makes it the first major party in the UK to recognise Zionism as a form of racism - and to back a single democratic Palestinian state with equal rights for all ethnic and religious groups, rather than a two-state solution.
1,022 members voted for the motion while 813 voted against it.
Co-Deputy Leader Mothin Ali told Middle East Eye on Sunday that he was strongly in favour of the motion, unlike Green MPs Carla Denyer and Adrian Ramsay, who criticised it.
"As defined in the motion," Ali said, "Zionism is an ethno-nationalist state. Zionism is resulting in ethnic cleansing, in the belief that one group of people is superior to another."

data.author: Katherine Hearst
data.summary:
Houthis claim attacks on Aramco sites in Saudi Arabia
The Houthi group has claimed a series of attacks on sites belonging to Saudi energy giant Aramco in Riyadh and the Khurais area in the east of the kingdom.
The Houthi military's spokesman Yahya Saree said in a statement on X that fighters had targeted the sites with ballistic missiles and drones, and that "both operations successfully achieved their objectives".
“The strikes were precise causing large fires at the targeted sites," Saree added, saying that the attacks came in response to Saudi strikes on Houthi-controlled areas of Yemen, warning of further attacks on Saudi military and energy sites.
“[The] enemy continues its unjust aggression against our people by launching more aggressive air strikes, which during the past 12 hours amounted to 50 air strikes and missiles targeting the capital, Sanaa, and the governorates of al-Jawf, Taiz, Amran, Hajjah, and Sadah,” said Saree.

data.title: Middle East Eye: US response to Hormuz proposal currently 'under review' by Tehran
data.author: Katherine Hearst
data.summary:
US response to Hormuz proposal currently 'under review' by Tehran
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has said a US response to a proposal put forward by Tehran is currently "under review".
Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi confirmed they had received a response via intermediaries to their proposal for a seven-day plan to reopen the contested Strait of Hormuz, which they presented at UN meetings in New York.
He added that "the Islamic Republic of Iran’s final response is prepared [and] the necessary steps will be taken through the appropriate channels".
US President Donald Trump said in late September that he had rejected the plan, but Iran has maintained that negotiations through mediators are ongoing.
Iran's Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said earlier today that the strait will remain shut until Washington meets seven conditions based on the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding.

data.title: Middle East Eye: ‘The Israeli occupation does not distinguish’: Gaza family mourns Christian mother and daughter
data.author: Katherine Hearst
data.summary:
‘The Israeli occupation does not distinguish’: Gaza family mourns Christian mother and daughter
Fourteen-year-old Fuad woke up at around 5am on Saturday at his father’s house to get ready for school.
He learned that his mother and grandmother had been killed in an Israeli air strike on their apartment in western Gaza City.
Mary Abu Dawud and her mother Maysaa were among the five Palestinians killed in the al-Asala residential building, after three strikes hit the area at around 1.30am, according to Palestinian authorities and church representatives.
“My mother was thrown against the wall by the force of the explosion, and my grandmother was engulfed in flames after the missile hit the house,” Fuad said.
“Today, I lost the most precious person in my life. There are no words to describe my feelings.”

data.author: Ayse Betul Aytekin
data.summary:
Over 70 dead in fighting around Yemen's Taiz in 24 hours
More than 70 people have been killed over the past day in fighting in and around the southwestern Yemeni province of Taiz, AFP reported on Sunday, citing sources from both sides.
Sources from the Yemeni government reported that 34 troops were killed, 20 of them in neighbouring Lahj, on the edge of Taiz province.
Houthi military sources said 39 of their fighters were killed in fighting across Taiz and in areas bordering Lahj.
The Yemeni government announced earlier on Sunday that it had launched a new wave of military operations to reclaim Houthi-controlled territory.
The same day, the Houthis cut a vital supply route linking Taiz with Aden, the interim capital of the internationally recognised government.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Iran airlines resume flights to Iraq’s Najaf after US exemption
data.author: Ayse Betul Aytekin
data.summary:
Iran airlines resume flights to Iraq’s Najaf after US exemption
Iranian airlines resumed flights to Iraq’s Najaf on Sunday after the United States granted Baghdad an exemption allowing sanctioned Iranian carriers to operate to the city holy to Shia Muslims, AFP reported.
On Friday, the Iraqi government said it had secured an agreement with the US allowing Iranian airlines, except Mahan Air, to operate 40 daily flights to and from Najaf.
Last month, Iraq enforced the US ban on Iranian carriers, especially at Najaf’s airport, which is a major hub for Iranian flights.
The US also granted Iraqi Airways, the national carrier, a waiver to fly between Najaf and Iran, with the flights expected to start this month.
